solution:
After reaching any of the letters $T, I, S, Z$, the next letter of the word can be chosen from 2 neighbors, meaning the reading can branch out in two ways at each letter. The letter $T$ appears once, so the word $T I S Z A$ can be read in $1 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 16$ ways.

To provide a solution for further questions, we also give a method that can be used for reading $TISZA$ in structures of different shapes. Write the number of ways to reach each letter of part a) of the diagram in place of the corresponding letter in part b), starting from $T$. For example, there is 1 way to reach $T$, 1 way to reach each $I$, 1 way to reach each outer $S$, 2 ways to reach the middle $S$ (via the two $I$s), and so on. Similarly, there are $1+2$ ways to reach each inner $Z$. The desired number is given by the sum of the numbers written at the $A$s.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_411e4e93bb3a15aacfc1g-1.jpg?height=268&width=1410&top_left_y=511&top_left_x=346)

Part c) of the diagram also answers in this way, but based on the somewhat peculiar observation: the number of ways to read $T I S Z A$ is the same as the number of ways to read $A Z S I T$ in reverse. The numbers in corresponding positions in parts b) and c) of the diagram - as shown in part d) - also give the number of readings that use each letter; for example, the $Z$ in the second column has $3 \cdot 2$ paths: 3 types of $T I S Z$ and 2 types of $A Z$ arrive at it, and each type of $T I S Z$ can be connected with each type of $Z A$. (The sum of the numbers in each diagonal row of the same type of letter gives the total number of readings.)

In reading the words $CSERE$ and $BERE$, a turn is possible at the $R$ in $CSEREBERE$, and at the $B$ in $BERE$; that is, after moving down and to the right, the last $E$ or the $B E R E$ segment can also be taken by moving up or to the left. The $CSEREBERE$ diagram is mapped onto itself by reflection in any of its diagonals, so it is enough to count the readings that start from the upper $C$ and use one of the $R$s in the 1st and 2nd columns; the desired number is clearly four times this. One and three paths lead to the mentioned $R$s, and the number of adjacent $E$s is 3 and 4, respectively, and we can move to all but one of them, i.e., the one we arrived from; thus, the incoming paths can be completed in 2 and 3 ways, respectively. The number of readings - including the symmetric cases: $4(1 \cdot 2 + 3 \cdot 3) = 44$ (with the idea of part d)).

The $BERE$ case differs from this only in that 4 paths lead to each $R$ - part c) - so the number of readings is $4(4 \cdot 2 + 4 \cdot 3) = 80$.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_411e4e93bb3a15aacfc1g-1.jpg?height=298&width=938&top_left_y=1504&top_left_x=539)

In the word $CSEREBERE$, a turn is only possible at the second $R$ and at the $B$. The total number of readings without turning and with turning only at the second $R$ is, following the pattern of $CSERE$, $4(21 \cdot 2 + 35 \cdot 3) = 588$. - To count the total number of readings with a turn at $B$, the different possibilities must be examined in more detail. It is enough to consider the $B$s in the 2nd and 3rd columns, as a turn is not possible at the corner $B$s. Of the 5 paths from the upper $C$ to the second $B$, 2 do not have a turning $BERE$ ending, and the other 3 have 1 and 2 endings, respectively, totaling 4. - To the third $B$, 4 paths arrive from the left and 6 from above. The paths arriving with a single direction change provide the most possibilities for the turning $BERE$ reading, 4 and 3, respectively. It is easy to count that 4, 3, 2, and 2 endings correspond to the paths arriving from the left, and 3, 2, 1, 2, 1, and 0 to those arriving from above, totaling 20, so the total number of $CSEREBERE$ readings with a turn at $B$ is $4(0 + 4 + 20) = 96$, and there are only 684 reading possibilities.

problem: 12.1.1. In a box, there are 6 identical pairs of black gloves and 4 identical pairs of beige gloves. Find the probability that two randomly drawn gloves form a pair.
solution:
Solution. Consider the event $A$ - two randomly drawn gloves form a pair; and hypotheses: $B_{1}$ - a pair of black gloves is drawn, $B_{2}$ - a pair of beige gloves is drawn, $B_{3}$ - the drawn gloves do not form a pair.

The probability of hypothesis $B_{1}$ by the multiplication theorem is the product of the probabilities that the first glove is black and the second glove is black, i.e.,

$$
P\left(B_{1}\right)=P_{1 \text { black }} \cdot P_{2 \text { black }}=\frac{12}{20} \cdot \frac{11}{19}=\frac{33}{95} .
$$

Similarly, the probability of hypothesis $B_{2}$ is:

$$
P\left(B_{2}\right)=P_{1 \text { beige }} \cdot P_{2 \text { beige }}=\frac{8}{20} \cdot \frac{7}{19}=\frac{14}{95} .
$$

Since hypotheses $B_{1}, B_{2}$, and $B_{3}$ form a complete set of events, the probability of hypothesis $B_{3}$ is:

$$
P\left(B_{3}\right)=1-\left(P\left(B_{1}\right)+P\left(B_{2}\right)\right)=1-\frac{33}{95}-\frac{14}{95}=\frac{48}{95}
$$

By the formula of total probability, we have:

$$
P(A)=P\left(B_{1}\right) \cdot P_{B_{1}}(A)+P\left(B_{2}\right) \cdot P_{B_{2}}(A)+P\left(B_{3}\right) \cdot P_{B_{3}}(A),
$$

where $P_{B_{1}}(A)$ is the probability that a pair of black gloves is formed and $P_{B_{1}}(A)=1$; $P_{B_{2}}(A)$ is the probability that a pair of beige gloves is formed and $P_{B_{2}}(A)=1$; and finally, $P_{B_{3}}(A)$ is the probability that a pair is formed by gloves of different colors and $P_{B_{3}}(A)=0$.

Substituting into the formula of total probability:

$$
P(A)=\frac{33}{95} \cdot 1+\frac{14}{95} \cdot 1+\frac{48}{95} \cdot 0=\frac{47}{95}
$$

Thus, the probability that two randomly drawn gloves form a pair is $\frac{47}{95}$.

problem:
Find the remainder of the Euclidean division of $x^{100}-2 x^{51}+1$ by $x^{2}-1$.

## - Roots and factorization of polynomials

Here we see that the knowledge of the roots of a polynomial allows us to factorize it. Recall that $\mathbb{K}$ denotes $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{Q}$.

Definition 1.10. An element $x \in \mathbb{K}$ is called a root of a polynomial $P \in \mathbb{K}[X]$ if $P(x)=0$.

Example 1.11. The real polynomial $X^{2}-1$ has two real roots, which are 1 and -1. The polynomial $X^{2}+1$ has no real roots. The real polynomial $X^{2}-2$ has two real roots, but the polynomial with rational coefficients $X^{2}-2$ has no rational roots because $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.

Theorem 1.12. Let $P \in \mathbb{K}[X]$ and $a \in \mathbb{K}$. The following two propositions are equivalent:

1. a is a root of $P$, that is, $P(a)=0$.
2. There exists a polynomial $Q \in \mathbb{K}[X]$ such that:

$$
P(x)=Q(x)(x-a) \text {. }
$$

Proof. It is clear that the second point implies the first. As for the converse, the key is to use Euclidean division. Indeed, suppose that $P(a)=0$. Then write the Euclidean division of $P$ by $X-a$ in the form $P(x)=Q(x)(x-a)+R(x)$ with $R$ a polynomial of degree at most $1-1=0$. Thus, $R$ is a real number, denoted by $c$. In short, $P(x)=Q(x)(x-a)+c$. Evaluate this quantity at $x=a: 0=P(a)=Q(a)(a-a)+c$. Therefore, $c=0$, which is what we wanted to prove.

Theorem 1.13. A polynomial of degree $n$ has at most $n$ different roots.

Proof. By contradiction, let $P \in \mathbb{R}[X]$ of degree $n$ having at least $n+1$ different roots, denoted $r_{1}, \ldots, r_{n+1}$. According to the previous theorem, there exists a polynomial $Q$ such that $P(x)=$ $Q(x)\left(x-r_{1}\right)$. But then, for $2 \leq i \leq n+1,0=P\left(r_{i}\right)=Q\left(r_{i}\right)\left(r_{i}-r_{1}\right)$. Since $r_{i}-r_{1} \neq 0$, this implies $Q\left(r_{i}\right)=0$. We repeat this reasoning with $Q$ to finally obtain the existence of a polynomial $T$ such that $P(x)=T(x)\left(x-r_{1}\right) \cdots\left(x-r_{n+1}\right)$. Then, according to Proposition 1.6:

$$
n=\operatorname{deg}(P)=\operatorname{deg} T+n+1>n
$$

which is absurd.

Remark 1.14. There exist polynomials that have no real roots, for example $P(x)=$ $x^{4}+1$.

This important theorem implies some corollaries giving information about the polynomial given something about its roots.

Corollary 1.15. Let $P(x)=a_{0}+a_{1} x+\cdots+a_{n} x^{n}$ be a polynomial of degree $n$. Suppose it has $n$ different roots $r_{1}, \ldots, r_{n}$. Then:

$$
P(x)=a_{n}\left(x-r_{1}\right) \cdots\left(x-r_{n}\right)
$$

Proof. By revisiting the previous proof, we see that there exists a polynomial $T$ such that $P(x)=T(x)\left(x-r_{1}\right) \cdots\left(x-r_{n}\right)$. By comparing the degrees of the terms on the left and right, it follows that $T$ is of degree zero, hence a real number. By looking at the leading coefficient on both sides of the equality, we find that $T(x)=a_{n}$.

Corollary 1.16. A polynomial of degree $n$ having $n+1$ roots is zero. Thus, a polynomial having an infinite number of roots is necessarily the zero polynomial.

problem:
Problem 1. Let $k \leq 2022$ be a positive integer. Alice and Bob play a game on a $2022 \times 2022$ board. Initially, all cells are white. Alice starts and the players alternate. In her turn, Alice can either color one white cell in red or pass her turn. In his turn, Bob can either color a $k \times k$ square of white cells in blue or pass his turn. Once both players pass, the game ends and the person who colored more cells wins (a draw can occur).

For each $1 \leq k \leq 2022$, determine which player (if any) has a winning strategy.

(David Hruška)
solution:
Solution. Answer: For $k \in\{1,3,337,1011\}$ the game ends in a draw, otherwise Alice wins.

Fix $k$. Number the rows from top to bottom and the columns from left to right using numbers $1, \ldots, 2022$. We say that a cell is critical if its row-number and column-number are both divisible by $k$. Note that Bob colors exactly one critical cell in each his turn. Let $c=\lfloor 2022 / k\rfloor^{2}$ be the number of critical cells.

We distinguish 3 cases based on the value 2022/k.

(1) $2022 / k \notin \mathbb{Z}$. Then Alice can force a win, e.g. by primarily coloring the critical cells (and then coloring the rest): If she follows this strategy then Bob will color a $k \times k$ square in at most $c / 2$ of his turns, so in total he will color $\frac{1}{2} c \cdot k^{2}<\frac{1}{2} \cdot 2022^{2}$ cells.

(2) $2022 / k$ is an odd integer. Then Alice can force a win by the same strategy: In this case $c$ is odd, so Bob will color a $k \times k$ square in at most $\lfloor c / 2\rfloor<\frac{1}{2} c$ of his turns, so in total he will color strictly less than $\frac{1}{2} c \cdot k^{2}=\frac{1}{2} \cdot 2022^{2}$ cells.

(3) $2022 / k$ is an even integer. Then both players can guarantee at least a draw: Alice by the above strategy, Bob by always coloring a $k \times k$ square whose bottom right corner cell is critical. Since in this case $c$ is even and each Alice's move prevents Bob from coloring at most 1 such square, using this strategy he will color at least $\frac{1}{2} c \cdot k^{2}=\frac{1}{2} \cdot 2022^{2}$ cells.

Since $2022=2 \cdot 3 \cdot 337$, case (3) occurs if and only if $k \in\{1,3,337,1011\}$.

## Solution.

Domain of definition: $a \neq 1$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{2 a^{4}+a^{3}+4 a^{2}+a+2}{2 a^{3}-a^{2}+a-2}=\frac{\left(2 a^{4}+2 a^{2}\right)+\left(a^{3}+a\right)+\left(2 a^{2}+2\right)}{\left(2 a^{3}-2 a^{2}\right)+\left(a^{2}-a\right)+(2 a-2)}= \\
& =\frac{2 a^{2}\left(a^{2}+1\right)+a\left(a^{2}+1\right)+2\left(a^{2}+1\right)}{2 a^{2}(a-1)+a(a-1)+2(a-1)}=\frac{\left(a^{2}+1\right)\left(2 a^{2}+a+2\right)}{(a-1)\left(2 a^{2}+a+2\right)}=\frac{a^{2}+1}{a-1} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Answer: $\frac{a^{2}+1}{a-1}$.

problem: 3. On the table, there are 140 different cards with numbers $4, 8, 12, \ldots, 556, 560$ (each card has exactly one number, and each number appears exactly once). In how many ways can 3 cards be chosen so that the sum of the numbers on the selected cards is divisible by 3?
solution:
Answer: 149224.

Solution. The given numbers, arranged in ascending order, form an arithmetic progression with a difference of 4. Therefore, the remainders of these numbers when divided by 3 alternate. Indeed, if one of these numbers is divisible by 3, i.e., has the form $3k$, where $k \in \mathbb{N}$, then the next number is $3k+4=3(k+1)+1$ - and it gives a remainder of 1 when divided by 3, followed by $3k+8=3(k+2)+2$, which gives a remainder of 2 when divided by 3, and then $-3k+12$, which is again divisible by 3. Thus, the remainders of the given numbers when divided by 3 go in the order $\ldots 0 ; 1 ; 2 ; 0 ; 1 ; 2 ; 0 \ldots$

Among the given numbers, there are 47 that give a remainder of 1 when divided by 3 (they form the set $A=\{4 ; 16 ; 28 ; \ldots ; 556\}$), 46 numbers that are divisible by 3 ($B=\{12 ; 24 ; 36 ; \ldots ; 552\}$), and 47 numbers that give a remainder of 2 when divided by 3 ($C=\{8 ; 20 ; 32 ; \ldots ; 560\}$).

The sum of three numbers can be divisible by 3 in the following cases.

1) All three numbers give the same remainder when divided by 3. There are $C_{46}^{3}$ ways to choose 3 numbers from set $B$ and $C_{47}^{3}$ ways to choose 3 numbers from sets $A$ and $C$. In total, we get $\frac{46 \cdot 45 \cdot 44}{6}+2 \cdot \frac{47 \cdot 46 \cdot 45}{6}=15180+2 \cdot 16215=47610$ ways.
2) If not all remainders are the same, then only the case where all three remainders are different fits, i.e., we must choose one number from each of the sets $A, B, C$. We get $47 \cdot 47 \cdot 46=$ 101614 ways.

In total, we get 149224 ways.

## Solution.

From the condition

Example 4. Integrate the equation

$$
x(x+2 y) d x+\left(x^{2}-y^{2}\right) d y=0
$$
solution:
Solution. In this case

$$
P(x, y)=x(x+2 y), Q(x, y)=x^{2}-y^{2}
$$

from which

$$
\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=2 x, \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}=2 x
$$

Condition (9.34) is satisfied, so the given equation is an equation in total differentials. Therefore,

$$
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=x^{2}+2 y x, \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=x^{2}-y^{2}
$$

From the first equality, we obtain

$$
u(x, y)=\int\left(x^{2}+2 x y\right) d x
$$

or

$$
u(x, y)=\frac{x^{3}}{3}+x^{2} y+\varphi(y)
$$

Differentiating the function $u(x, y)$ with respect to $y$, we find

$$
\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=x^{2}+\varphi^{\prime}(y)
$$

Since

$$
\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=x^{2}-y^{2}
$$

then

$$
x^{2}+\varphi^{\prime}(y)=x^{2}-y^{2}
$$

from which

$$
\varphi^{\prime}(y)=-y^{2}
$$

and

$$
\varphi(y)=-\int y^{2} d y=-\frac{y^{3}}{3}+C_{1}
$$

Substituting the found expression for $\varphi(y)$ into the formula for $u(x, y)$, we get

$$
u(x, y)=\frac{x^{3}}{3}+x^{2} y-\frac{y^{3}}{3}+C_{1}=C_{2}
$$

or

$$
\frac{x^{3}}{3}+x^{2} y-\frac{y^{3}}{3}=C_{3}
$$

Thus, the general integral can be written in the form

$$
x^{3}+3 x^{2} y-y^{3}=C, \text { where } C=3 C_{3}
$$

problem: Example 5 (2005 National High School Mathematics League Test Question) Define the function $f(k)=\left\{\begin{array}{l}0, k \text { is a perfect square } \\ {\left[\frac{1}{\{\sqrt{k}\}}\right], k \text { is not a perfect square, }}\end{array}\right.$ Find $\sum_{k=1}^{240} f(k)$.
solution:
Solve $15^{2}<240<16^{2}$.
Since $k$ is a perfect square when $f(k)=0$, we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=1}^{240} f(k) & =\sum_{k=1+1}^{2^{2}-1} f(k)+\sum_{k=2^{2}+1}^{3^{2}-1} f(k)+\cdots+\sum_{k=14^{2}+1}^{15^{2}-1} f(k)+\sum_{k=226}^{240} f(k) \\
& =\sum_{n=1}^{14} \sum_{k=n^{2}+1}^{(n+1)^{2}-1} f(k)+\sum_{k=226}^{240} f(k) .
\end{aligned}
$$

When $n^{2}+1 \leqslant k \leqslant(n+1)^{2}-1$, $[\sqrt{k}]=n,\{k\}=\sqrt{k}-[k]=\sqrt{k}-n$.
Thus, $\left[\frac{1}{\{\sqrt{k}\}}\right]=\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}-n}\right]=\left[\frac{\sqrt{k}+n}{k-n^{2}}\right]=\left[\frac{[\sqrt{k}+n]}{k-n^{2}}\right]=\left[\frac{2 n}{k-n^{2}}\right]$.
Therefore, $\sum_{k=n^{2}+1}^{(n+1)^{2}-1} f(k)=\sum_{k=n^{2}+1}^{(n+1)^{2}-1}\left[\frac{2 n}{k-n^{2}}\right]=\sum_{i=1}^{2 n}\left[\frac{2 n}{i}\right]$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=226}^{240} f(k) & =\sum_{k=226}^{240}\left[\frac{2 \cdot 15}{k-15^{2}}\right]=\sum_{i=1}^{15}\left[\frac{30}{i}\right] . \\
\text { Hence } \sum_{k=1}^{240} f(k) & =\sum_{n=1}^{14} \sum_{i=1}^{2 n}\left[\frac{2 n}{i}\right]+\sum_{i=1}^{15}\left[\frac{30}{i}\right] \\
& =\sum_{n=1}^{14}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\frac{2 n}{i}\right]+\sum_{i=n+1}^{2 n}\left[\frac{2 n}{i}\right]\right)+\sum_{i=1}^{15}\left[\frac{30}{i}\right] \\
& =\sum_{n=1}^{14}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\frac{2 n}{i}\right]+n\right)+\sum_{i=1}^{15}\left[\frac{30}{i}\right] \\
& =\sum_{n=1}^{14} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\frac{2 n}{i}\right]+\sum_{i=1}^{15}\left[\frac{30}{i}\right]+\sum_{n=1}^{14} n \\
& =\sum_{n=1}^{15} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\frac{2 n}{i}\right]+105 .
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $T_{n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\frac{2 n}{i}\right], 1 \leqslant n \leqslant 15$.
Then $T_{1}=\left[\frac{2}{1}\right]=2, T_{2}=\left[\frac{4}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{4}{2}\right]=4+2=6$,
$$
\begin{array}{l}
T_{3}=\left[\frac{6}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{6}{2}\right]+\left[\frac{6}{3}\right]=6+3+2=11, \\
T_{4}=\left[\frac{8}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{8}{2}\right]+\left[\frac{8}{3}\right]+\left[\frac{8}{4}\right]=8+4+2 \times 2=16, \\
T_{5}=\left[\frac{10}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{10}{2}\right]+\cdots+\left[\frac{10}{5}\right]=10+5+3+2 \times 2=22, \\
T_{6}=\left[\frac{12}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{12}{2}\right]+\cdots+\left[\frac{12}{6}\right]=12+6+4+3+2 \times 2=29, \\
T_{7}=\left[\frac{14}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{14}{2}\right]+\cdots+\left[\frac{14}{7}\right]=14+7+4+3+2 \times 3=34, \\
T_{8}=\left[\frac{16}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{16}{2}\right]+\cdots+\left[\frac{16}{8}\right]=16+8+5+4+3+2 \times 3=42, \\
T_{9}=\left[\frac{18}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{18}{2}\right]+\cdots+\left[\frac{18}{9}\right]=18+9+6+4+3 \times 2+2 \times 3=49, \\
T_{10}=\left[\frac{20}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{20}{2}\right]+\cdots+\left[\frac{20}{10}\right]=20+10+6+5+4+3+2 \times 4=56, \\
T_{11}=\left[\frac{22}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{22}{2}\right]+\cdots+\left[\frac{22}{11}\right]=22+11+7+5+4+3 \times 2+2 \times 4=63, \\
T_{12}=\left[\frac{24}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{24}{2}\right]+\cdots+\left[\frac{24}{12}\right]=24+12+8+6+4 \times 2+3 \times 2+2 \times 4=72, \\
T_{13}=\left[\frac{26}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{26}{2}\right]+\cdots+\left[\frac{26}{13}\right]=26+13+8+6+5+4+3 \times 2+2 \times 5=78, \\
T_{14}=\left[\frac{28}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{28}{2}\right]+\cdots+\left[\frac{28}{14}\right]=28+14+9+7+5+4 \times 2+3 \times 2+2 \times 5=87, \\
T_{15}=\left[\frac{30}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{30}{2}\right]+\cdots+\left[\frac{30}{15}\right]=30+15+10+7+6+5+4+3 \times 3+2 \times 5=96, \\
\text { Hence } \sum_{k=1}^{240} f(k)=\sum_{n=1}^{15} T_{n}+105 \\
=2+6+11+16+22+29+34+42+49+56+63+72+78+87+96+105 \\
=768.
\end{array}
$$

solution:

$$
\begin{gathered}

problem: Putnam 1997 Problem B3 Let (1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ... + 1/n) = p n /q n , where p n and q n are relatively prime positive integers. For which n is q n not divisible by 5? Solution
solution: : n = 1 - 4, 20 - 24, 100 - 104, and 120 - 124. Hard. I found this the trickiest problem in the paper. The key is to show that p n is not divisible by 5 for n = 25, ... , 124. Let S(n) = 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ... + 1/n, and let S'(n) be the same sum excluding terms 1/m with m a multiple of 5. For x non-integral it is convenient to use S(x) to mean S([x]). We find that S(1) = 1/1, S(2) = 3/2, S(3) = 11/6, S(4) = 25/12. Let N, N' etc denote fractions p/q where 5 does not divide q, let F, F' etc denote fractions p/q where 5 divides q, but not p, and let X, X' etc denote fractions p/q where 5 does not divide p or q. For example, we obviously have S'(n) = N. Notice that 1/(5r+1) + 1/(5r+2) + 1/(5r+3) + 1/(5r+4) = (1/(5r+1) + 1/(5r+4) ) + (1/(5r+2) + 1/(5r+3) ) = (10r+5)(1/(5r'+4) + 1/(5r''+6) ) = 25 N. So for n = 4 or 5 (mod 5) we have 1/5 S'(n) = 5N. For n = 5, ... , 19, S(n) = S'(n) + 1/5 S(n/5) = N + 1/5 X = F. For n = 20, ... ,24, S(n) = S'(n) + 1/5 25/12 = N + N' = N''. We need also that S(21) = S'(20) + 1/21 + 5/12 = 5N + 1/21 + 5N' = X, and similarly that S(22) = 5N + 1/21 + 1/22 = X, S(23) = 5N + 1/21 + 1/22 + 1/23 = X. For n = 25, ... , 99, S(n) = S'(n) + 1/5 S'(n/5) + 1/25 S(n/25) = N + 1/5 N' + 1/25 X = F. For n = 100, ... , 104, S(n) = S'(n) + 1/5 S'(20) + 1/25 25/12 = N + 5N' + 1/12 = N. But S'(100) = 5N, so we have the stronger result that S(100) = 5N'' + 1/12 = X. Similarly for S'(104). S(101) = S(100) + 1/101 = 5N'' + 1/12 + 1/101 = X (just check that the numerator of 1/12 + 1/101 is not a multiple of 5) and, similarly, S(102) = X, S(103) = X. For n = 105, ... , 119, S(n) = S'(n) + 1/5 S'(n/5) + 1/12 = N + 1/5 X + 1/12 = F (since S'(n/5) = S'(21) or S'(22) or S'(23) = X). For n = 120, ... , 124, S(n) = S'(n) + 1/5 S'(24) + 1/12 = N + 5N' + 1/12 = N. Exactly as for 100-104, we also have the stronger result that S(n) = X. We have established that S(n) has the denominator divisible by 5 for n = 1-4, 20-24, 100-104 and 120- 124. It remains to show that the denominator is not divisible by 5 for n ≥ 125. But we have also established that the numerator is not divisible by 5 for 25 ≤ n ≤ 124. So let n ≥ 125, and let h be the highest power of 5 not exceeding n, so h ≥ 3. We now divide S(n) into A, the sum of terms which are multiples of 5 h-2 and B, the sum of the remaining terms. Clearly B = N/5 h-3 . But A = S(r)/5 h-2 , where 25 ≤ r ≤ 124. But the numerator of S(r) is not divisible by 5, so the denominator of A is divisible by at least 5 h-2 and hence S(n) = A + B has denominator (in lowest terms) divisible by at least 5 h-2 and hence by 5. 3. Squaring both sides of $|5 x+y|+|5 x-y|=20$, and simplifying, we get $25 x^{2}+y^{2}+\left|25 x^{2}-y^{2}\right|=200$. If $|5 x|>|y|$, then we get $50 x^{2}=200, x= \pm 2,|y| \leqslant 10$; if $|5 x| \leqslant|y|$, then we get $2 y^{2}=200, y= \pm 10,|5 x| \leqslant 10,|x| \leqslant$ 2. problem:
# Problem 2. 15 points

It is known that the tangents to the graph of the target function $y=a(x+1)^{2}+1$, drawn from the point $M\left(x_{0} ; y_{0}\right)$, intersect at a right angle. Restore the form of the target function, given that the coordinates of the point $M\left(x_{0} ; y_{0}\right)$ satisfy the relation: $\log _{3 x-x^{2}+1}(y-4)=\log _{3 x-x^{2}+1} \frac{|2 x+4|-|2 x+1|}{3 x+4.5} \sqrt{x^{2}+3 x+2.25}$.
solution:
# Solution

Transform $y-1=a(x+1)^{2}$ and substitute $u=y-1 ; z=x+1$ so that $u=a z^{2}$. Let $A\left(z_{1} ; a z_{1}\right)$ and $B\left(z_{2} ; a z_{2}\right)$ be points on the parabola $u=a z^{2}$, and let the tangents at points $A$ and $B$ intersect at point $\left(z_{0} ; u_{0}\right)$.

Write the equation of the tangent at point $A: u-u_{1}=2 a z_{1}\left(z-z_{1}\right)$, where $u_{1}=a z_{1}^{2}$.

Since this line passes through the point $\left(z_{0} ; u_{0}\right)$, we have $u_{0}-a z_{1}^{2}=2 a z_{1}\left(z_{0}-z_{1}\right)$ or $u_{0}=2 a z_{0} z_{1}-a z_{1}^{2}$.

Similarly, we obtain the relation for the tangent at point $B: u_{0}=2 a z_{0} z_{2}-a z_{2}^{2}$.

Subtracting these relations, we get: $z_{0}=\frac{z_{1}+z_{2}}{2}$. Substituting this value into one of the previous relations, we get: $u_{0}=a z_{1} z_{2}$.

For the slopes of perpendicular lines, we have: $-1=k_{1} k_{2}=2 a z_{1} 2 a z_{2}=4 a u_{0}$.

From this, $a=-\frac{1}{4 u_{0}}=-\frac{1}{4\left(y_{0}-1\right)}$.

The value of $y_{0}$ is found from the relation:

$\log _{3 x-x^{2}+1}(y-4)=\log _{3 x-x^{2}+1} \frac{|2 x+4|-|2 x+1|}{3 x+4.5} \sqrt{x^{2}+3 x+2.25}$.

Domain: $\mathrm{y}>4 ; 3 x-x^{2}+1>0 ; \frac{|2 x+4|-|2 x+1|}{3 x+4.5} \sqrt{x^{2}+3 x+2.25}>0$

And further: $\left\{\begin{array}{l}y>4 \\ x \in\left(\frac{3-\sqrt{13}}{2} ; \frac{3+\sqrt{13}}{2}\right) .\end{array}\right.$

Exponentiating the logarithmic expression, we get: $y-4=\frac{|x+2|-|x+0.5|}{1.5} \cdot \frac{|x+1.5|}{x+1.5}$.

The expression on the right takes the value 1 in the domain of definition. Thus, we obtain:

$\left\{\begin{array}{l}y_{0}-4=1 \\ x_{0} \in\left(\frac{3-\sqrt{13}}{2} ; \frac{3+\sqrt{13}}{2}\right) . \text { From this, we have: } a=-\frac{1}{4\left(y_{0}-1\right)}=-\frac{1}{16}=-0.0625\end{array}\right.$

and the function

$y=-0.0625(x+1)^{2}+1$

Answer: $y=-0.0625(x+1)^{2}+1$

- correct solution and correct answer (form of the function) - 15 points,
- correct solution but incorrect answer or no answer - 8 points,
- error in the solution but correct answer (form of the function) - 7 points,
- incorrect solution or no solution, but correct answer (form of the function) - 1 point,
- incorrect solution or no solution, and incorrect answer or no answer - 0 points.

The roots of the given equations:

If these roots are ordered by magnitude, then:

The arithmetic progression of the consecutive terms is thus:

problem:
4. We will write down all five-digit numbers in which each of the digits $4,5,6,7,8$ appears exactly once. Then we will strike out one (any of them) and sum all the remaining ones. What are the possible values of the digital sum of such a result?

The regional round of category B takes place

## on Tuesday, April 5, 2011

so that it starts in the morning and the contestants have 4 hours of clean time to solve the problems. For each problem, a contestant can earn 6 points, and a successful solver is a student who scores 10 points or more. Allowed aids are writing and drawing supplies, school MF tables, and calculators without a graphical display. These details will be communicated to the students before the start of the competition.
solution:
4. The final digit sum is uniquely determined and is the number 33.

To solve the problem, it will be advantageous to first determine the sum $S$ of all five-digit numbers containing each of the digits $4,5,6,7,8$. There are clearly as many such numbers as there are different permutations of the five digits, i.e., $5!=120$. Moreover, each of the given digits appears equally in each position among these 120 numbers, i.e., 24 times. The sum $S$ can thus be broken down by individual positions as

$$
\begin{aligned}
S= & 10^{4} \cdot(24 \cdot 4+24 \cdot 5+24 \cdot 6+24 \cdot 7+24 \cdot 8)+ \\
& +10^{3} \cdot(24 \cdot 4+24 \cdot 5+24 \cdot 6+24 \cdot 7+24 \cdot 8)+\ldots= \\
= & 24 \cdot(4+5+6+7+8) \cdot\left(10^{4}+10^{3}+10^{2}+10+1\right)=24 \cdot 30 \cdot 11111 .
\end{aligned}
$$

Let us now turn our attention to the possible values of the digit sum of the number $S-a$, where $a$ is a five-digit number of the mentioned form, i.e., $a=33333+b$, where $b$ is a five-digit number containing each of the digits $1,2,3,4,5$. Thus,

$$
S-a=11111 \cdot 24 \cdot 30-a=7999920-33333-b=7966587-b .
$$

However, when subtracting the number $b$, there is no carry-over in the individual positions, so the digit sum of the number $S-a$ is equal to $(7+9+6+6+5+8+7)-(1+2+3+4+5)=48-15=33$ for any five-digit number $a$ containing each of the digits $4,5,6,7,8$.

For a complete solution, award 6 points.

problem:
1.28 Given $x, y \in N$, find the largest $y$ value such that there exists a unique $x$ value satisfying the following inequality:
$$
\frac{9}{17}<\frac{x}{x+y}<\frac{8}{15} \text {. }
$$
(Wuhan, Hubei Province, China Mathematical Summer Camp, 1987)
solution:
[Solution 1] Since $x, y \in N$, the given inequality can be transformed into
$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
8 x-9 y>0, \\
7 x-8 y<0 .
\end{array}\right.
$$

For the interval $\left(\frac{9 y}{8}, \frac{8 y}{7}\right)$ to contain a unique integer $x$, the necessary and sufficient conditions are:
(1) If $\frac{8 y}{7} \in N$, then $\frac{8 y}{7}=\left[\frac{9 y}{8}\right]+2$, or
(2) If $\frac{8 y}{7} \notin N$, then $\left[\frac{8 y}{7}\right]=\left[\frac{9 y}{8}\right]+1$.
Let $y=8 t+r, t \in N, r=0,1,2, \cdots, 7$.
From (1), we have
$$
9 t+\frac{t+8 r}{7}=9 t+\left[\frac{9 r}{8}\right]+2
$$

which simplifies to
$$
\frac{t+r}{7}=\left[\frac{r}{8}\right]+2
$$

Since $\left[\frac{r}{8}\right]=0$, we have
$$
\frac{t+r}{7} \in N, \quad t \in N .
$$

Thus,
$$
t+r=14.
$$

To maximize $y$, we take $r=0$.
Therefore,
$$
t=14, \quad y=112.
$$

The corresponding $x=127$ is the unique integer.
From (2), we have
$$
\left[\frac{t+r}{7}\right]=\left[\frac{r}{8}\right]+1=1,
$$

so we can take the maximum $t+r=13$,
To maximize $y$, we take $r=0, \quad t=13$,
In this case, $y$ is maximized at 104, with the corresponding $x=118$.
From the above, the maximum value of $y$ is 112.
[Solution 2] The original inequality can be transformed into
$$
\frac{15}{8}<\frac{x+y}{x}<\frac{17}{9}
$$

which simplifies to
$$
\begin{array}{c}
\frac{7}{8}<\frac{y}{x}<\frac{8}{9} \\
63 y<56 x<64 y .
\end{array}
$$

Thus, the problem is to find the largest open interval $(63 y, 64 y)$ that contains only one multiple of 56. Since the interval length is $y$, it contains $y-1$ integers.
If $y-1 \geqslant 2 \cdot 56$, then the interval must contain at least 2 multiples of 56.
Therefore, $y-1<2 \cdot 56$, which means $y \leqslant 112$.
When $y=112$, we have
$$
63 \cdot 112=126 \cdot 56<127 \cdot 56<128 \cdot 56=64 \cdot 112,
$$

where $x=127$, so $y=112$ is the solution.

Then \(a+b=3 b+5\) is not divisible by three, so (3) is false. Therefore, (1) and (4) must be true.

From (2), it follows that \(a+1=2 b+6\), and with (1), this is satisfied if and only if \(b \mid 6\), i.e., \(b \in\{1,2,3,6\}\).

Due to (2), \(a+7 b=9 b+5\). Therefore, \(a+7 b\) can only be prime if \(b\) is even. For \(b=2\), this is the case, since \(9 \cdot 2+5=23\) is prime. For \(b=6\) as well: \(9 \cdot 6+5=59\) is prime.

Thus, \((a, b)=(9,2)\) and \((a, b)=(17,6)\) are all the desired pairs.

problem:
7. (1995 China Mathematical Olympiad) Let $\mathbf{N}$ be the set of natural numbers. Let $f: \mathbf{N} \rightarrow \mathbf{N}$ satisfy the conditions: $f(1)=1$, and for any natural number $n$,
$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
3 f(n) f(2 n+1)=f(2 n)(1+3 f(n)), \\
f(2 n)<6 f(n) .
\end{array}\right.
$$

Find all solutions to the equation
$$
f(k)+f(l)=293, k<l
$$
solution:
7. From the conditions, for all $n \in \mathbf{N}$, we have
$$
1 \leqslant 3 f(n)(f(2 n+1)-f(2 n))=f(2 n)<6 f(n) .
$$

Therefore,
$$
\begin{array}{l}
1 \leqslant f(2 n+1)-f(2 n)<2, \\
f(2 n+1)=f(2 n)+1
\end{array}
$$

Substituting (2) into (1) gives
$$
f(2 n)=3 f(n) .
$$

Using (2) and (3), we can prove by mathematical induction that
$$
f\left(2^{n_{1}}+2^{n_{2}}+\cdots+2^{n}\right)=3^{n_{1}}+3^{n_{2}}+\cdots+3^{n_{s}},
$$

where the non-negative integers $n_{1}, n_{2}, \cdots, n_{s}$ satisfy
$$
\begin{array}{l}
0 \leqslant n_{1}<n_{2}<\cdots<n_{s} . \\
\text { Let } \quad k=2^{n_{1}}+2^{n_{2}}+\cdots+2^{n}, \\
l=2^{m_{1}}+2^{m_{2}}+\cdots+2^{m_{t}},
\end{array}
$$

where $n_{1}<n_{2}<\cdots<n_{s}, m_{1}<m_{2}<\cdots<m_{t}$.
When $k<l$, it is clear that $f(k)<f(l)$. Note that
$$
293=3^{5}+3^{3}+2 \times 3^{2}+3+2 \times 3^{0},
$$

where $3^{5}=243$ must be one of the addends of $f(l)$, and $3^{2}$ and $3^{0}$ must be addends in both $f(k)$ and $f(l)$, while $3^{3}$ and 3 are uncertain. Therefore, $f(k)$ and $f(l)$ can only have the following 4 cases:
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
f(k)=3^{2}+3^{0}, \\
f(l)=3^{5}+3^{3}+3^{2}+3+3^{10} ;
\end{array}\right. \\
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
f(k)=3^{3}+3^{2}+3^{10}, \\
f(l)=3^{5}+3^{2}+3+3^{0} ;
\end{array}\right. \\
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
f(k)=3^{2}+3+3^{0}, \\
f(l)=3^{5}+3^{3}+3^{2}+3^{0} ;
\end{array}\right. \\
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
f(k)=3^{3}+3^{2}+3+3^{0}, \\
f(l)=3^{5}+3^{2}+3^{0} .
\end{array}\right.
\end{array}
$$

Accordingly, we obtain all solutions to the given equation:
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
k=2^{2}+2^{0}=5, \\
l=2^{5}+2^{3}+2^{2}+2+1=47 ;
\end{array}\right. \\
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
k=2^{3}+2^{2}+2^{0}=13, \\
l=2^{5}+2^{2}+2+2^{0}=39 ;
\end{array}\right. \\
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
k=2^{2}+2+2^{0}=7, \\
l=2^{5}+2^{3}+2^{2}+2^{0}=45 ;
\end{array}\right. \\
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
k=2^{3}+2^{2}+2+2^{0}=15, \\
l=2^{5}+2^{3}+2^{\prime \prime}=37 .
\end{array}\right.

$$

problem: Question 216, Given $2^{2013}<5^{867}<2^{2014}$, how many integer pairs $(\mathrm{m}, \mathrm{n})$ satisfy: $5^{\mathrm{n}}<2^{\mathrm{m}}<$ $2^{\mathrm{m}+2}<5^{\mathrm{n}+1}$ ~ where $1 \leq \mathrm{m} \leq 2012$.
solution:
Question 216, Solution: First, we prove that for any non-negative integer $n$, the interval $\left(5^{n}, 5^{n+1}\right)$ contains either two or three powers of 2.

If there exists a non-negative integer $n$ such that the interval $\left(5^{n}, 5^{n+1}\right)$ contains only one power of 2, let's say $2^{m}$, then $2^{m-1} \leq 5^{n}\frac{5^{n+1}}{5^{n}}=5$, which is impossible; if there exists a non-negative integer $n$ such that the interval $\left(5^{n}, 5^{n+1}\right)$ contains at least four powers of 2, let's say $5^{n}\frac{2^{m+3}}{2^{m}}=8$, which is also impossible. Therefore, the above statement is proven.

Returning to the original problem, according to the conditions, we know that $2^{2012}<2^{2013}<5^{867}<2^{2014}$. We need to find how many of the 867 intervals $\left(5^{0}, 5^{1}\right)$, $\left(5^{1}, 5^{2}\right), \cdots,\left(5^{866}, 5^{867}\right)$ contain exactly three powers of 2. Let's say there are $\mathrm{m}$ intervals that contain exactly three powers of 2, and $\mathrm{n}$ intervals that contain exactly two powers of 2. Then $\left\{\begin{array}{c}m+n=867 \\ 3 m+2 n=2013\end{array}\right.$, solving this gives $m=279$.

problem:
## Problem Statement

Calculate the definite integral:

$$
\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{2 \operatorname{arctan} 2} \frac{d x}{\sin ^{2} x(1+\cos x)}
$$
solution:
## Solution

We will use the universal substitution:

$$
t=\operatorname{tg} \frac{x}{2}
$$

From which:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sin x=\frac{2 t}{1+t^{2}}, \cos x=\frac{1-t^{2}}{1+t^{2}}, d x=\frac{2 d t}{1+t^{2}} \\
& x=\frac{\pi}{2} \Rightarrow t=\operatorname{tg} \frac{\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)}{2}=\operatorname{tg} \frac{\pi}{4}=1 \\
& x=2 \operatorname{arctg} 2 \Rightarrow t=\operatorname{tg} \frac{2 \operatorname{arctg} 2}{2}=\operatorname{tg}(\operatorname{arctg} 2)=2
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{2 \operatorname{arctg} 2} \frac{d x}{\sin ^{2} x(1+\cos x)}=\int_{1}^{2} \frac{\frac{2 d t}{1+t^{2}}}{\left(\frac{2 t}{1+t^{2}}\right)^{2} \cdot\left(1+\frac{1-t^{2}}{1+t^{2}}\right)}= \\
& =\int_{1}^{2} \frac{\frac{2 d t}{1+t^{2}}}{\frac{4 t^{2}}{\left(1+t^{2}\right)^{2}} \cdot \frac{1+t^{2}+1-t^{2}}{1+t^{2}}}=\int_{1}^{2} \frac{d t}{\frac{2 t^{2}}{1+t^{2}} \cdot \frac{2}{1+t^{2}}}=\int_{1}^{2} \frac{\left(1+t^{2}\right)^{2} d t}{4 t^{2}}= \\
& =\int_{1}^{2} \frac{1+2 t^{2}+t^{4}}{4 t^{2}} d t=\int_{1}^{2}\left(\frac{1}{4 t^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}+\frac{t^{2}}{4}\right) d t= \\
& =-\frac{1}{4 t}+\frac{t}{2}+\left.\frac{t^{3}}{12}\right|_{1} ^{2}=\left(-\frac{1}{4 \cdot 2}+\frac{2}{2}+\frac{2^{3}}{12}\right)-\left(-\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1^{3}}{12}\right)= \\
& =-\frac{1}{8}+1+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{12}=\frac{29}{24}=1 \frac{5}{24}
\end{aligned}
$$

10. (20 points) In the first month, there is a pair of adult rabbits. Every month, they breed 3 male rabbits and 2 female rabbits. The young female rabbits grow up and also breed 3 male rabbits and 2 female rabbits every other month. Question: How many rabbits will there be in the $n$ $\left(n \in \mathbf{Z}_{+}\right)$-th month?
solution:
10. Let $a_{n}$ denote the number of male rabbits in the $n$-th month, and $b_{n}$ denote the number of female rabbits in the $n$-th month. Then, from the problem statement, we have
$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
a_{n}=a_{n-1}+3 b_{n-2}, \\
b_{n}=b_{n-1}+2 b_{n-2},
\end{array}\right.
$$

where $n \geqslant 2, a_{0}=1, a_{1}=4, b_{0}=1, b_{1}=3$.
Solving this, we get $a_{n}=2^{n+1}-\frac{1-(-1)^{n-1}}{2}$,
$$
b_{n}=\frac{2^{n+2}-(-1)^{n}}{3} \text {. }
$$

Then $a_{n}+b_{n}$
$$
\begin{array}{l}
=2^{n+1}-\frac{1-(-1)^{n-1}}{2}+\frac{2^{n+2}-(-1)^{n}}{3} \\
=\frac{5 \times 2^{n+2}-5(-1)^{n}-3}{6} .
\end{array}
$$

Therefore, after the $n$-th month, there are $\frac{5 \times 2^{n+2}-5(-1)^{n}-3}{6}$ rabbits.

problem: A $0,1,3,5,6$ digits can form how many different four-digit numbers, all digits being distinct, that are divisible by 15?
solution:
Numbers divisible by 15 are those divisible by 5 and 3, meaning they end in 0 or 5, and the sum of their digits is divisible by 3. Due to the latter condition, only the following groups of digits meet the criteria: a) $1,3,5,6$, b) $0,1,5,6$, and c) $0,1,3,5$.

In case a), the number of numbers ending in 5 is $3!=6$.

In case b), the number of numbers ending in 0 is $3!=6$, and the number of numbers ending in 5 is $3!-2!=4$, because we must exclude the groups starting with 0.

In case c), similarly to case b), $6+4=10$ numbers can be formed that meet our conditions.

Therefore, a total of $6+10+10=26$ numbers, each with distinct digits, can be formed from the given digits that are divisible by 15.

Beke Éva and Mária (Bp. XIII., Ép. gép. techn. II. o. t)

Solve the equation

$$
\frac{(n+2)!-(n+1)!-n!}{n!}=2024
$$
solution:
## Solution.

Let's write all factorials in the numerator of the given expression using $n$ !:

$$
\frac{(n+2)(n+1) n!-(n+1) n!-n!}{n!}=2024
$$

Now we can divide both the numerator and the denominator of the given fraction by $n$ !. It follows that:

$$
(n+2)(n+1)-(n+1)-1=2024
$$

and after simplification, we get the quadratic equation $n^{2}+2 n-2024=0$.

Its solutions are -46 and 44. Since we are dealing with factorials, the number $n$ must be a natural number, so the only possible solution is $n=44$.

problem:
## Problem A1

What is the smallest number of colors needed to color 8 boxes of 6 balls (one color for each ball), so that the balls in each box are all different colors and any pair of colors occurs in at most one box.
solution:
## Solution

If each color occurs only twice, then we need at least $8 \cdot 6 / 2=24$ colors. But we can do better, so at least one color occurs more than twice.

If a color occurs 4 times or more, let the first 4 boxes each include it. Then those 4 boxes use $1+4 \cdot 5=21$ colors. Now the 5th box can use at most one color from each of the first 4 boxes, so it must use another 2 colors as well. Now the 6th box can use at most one color from each of the first 5 boxes, so it must use another color as well. We are now up to 24 colors. But we can do better.

problem: Example: There are 3 bags with 10 balls each of red, white, and black. If 16 balls are drawn from them, and it is required that all three colors are included, how many different ways are there to do this?
solution:
Assume the total number of ways to take out $n$ balls is $a_{n}$, where the number of red, white, and black balls are $x_{1}$, $x_{2}$, and $x_{3}$ respectively, then $a_{n}=\sum_{x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}=n} 1\left(x_{i}\right.$ are positive integers, $\left.1 \leqslant x_{i} \leqslant 10, i=1,2,3\right)$, thus the generating function of $a_{n}$ is
$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x) & =\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_{n} x^{n}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(\sum_{x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}=n} 1\right) x^{n}=\sum_{x_{1}=1}^{10} \sum_{x_{2}=1}^{10} \sum_{x_{3}=1}^{10} x^{x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}} \\
& =\left(\sum_{x_{1}=1}^{10} x^{x_{1}}\right)\left(\sum_{x_{2}=1}^{10} x^{x_{2}}\right)\left(\sum_{x_{3}=1}^{10} x^{x_{3}}\right)=\left(x+x^{2}+\cdots+x^{10}\right)^{3}=\frac{x^{3}\left(1-x^{10}\right)^{3}}{(1-x)^{3}} \\
& =x^{3}\left(1-3 x^{10}+3 x^{20}-x^{30}\right) \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} C_{n+2}^{2} x^{n}
\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficient of $x^{16}$ is
$$
a_{16}=C_{13+2}^{2}-3 C_{3+2}^{2}=105-30=75 .
$$

Thus, there are 75 different ways to take out the balls.

problem:
Solve the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a^{3} x+a^{2} y+a z+u & =1 \\
b^{3} x+b^{2} y+b z+u & =0 \\
c^{3} x+c^{2} y+c z+u & =0 \\
d^{3} x+d^{2} y+d z+u & =0
\end{aligned}
$$
solution:
First, we calculate a few determinants that we will need. The determinant of the system of equations is:

$$
D=\left|\begin{array}{llll}
a^{3} & a^{2} & a & 1 \\
b^{3} & b^{2} & b & 1 \\
c^{3} & c^{2} & c & 1 \\
d^{3} & d^{2} & d & 1
\end{array}\right|
$$

Subtract the elements of the last row from the corresponding elements of the first three rows, then:

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_109b1469a5295e62460dg-1.jpg?height=195&width=1193&top_left_y=474&top_left_x=455)

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =(a-d)(b-d)(c-d)\left|\begin{array}{lll}
a^{2} & a & 1 \\
b^{2} & b & 1 \\
c^{2} & c & 1
\end{array}\right|=(a-d)(b-d)(c-d)\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
a^{2}-c^{2} & a-c & 0 \\
b^{2}-c^{2} & b-c & 0 \\
c^{2} & c & 1
\end{array}\right|= \\
& =(a-c)(a-d)(b-c)(b-d)(c-d)\left|\begin{array}{ll}
a+c & 1 \\
b+c & 1
\end{array}\right|=(a-b)(a-c)(a-d)(b-c)(b-d)(c-d)
\end{aligned}
$$

Furthermore:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& D_{1}=\left|\begin{array}{llll}
1 & a^{2} & a & 1 \\
0 & b^{2} & b & 1 \\
0 & c^{2} & c & 1 \\
0 & d^{2} & d & 1
\end{array}\right|=\left|\begin{array}{lll}
b^{2} & b & 1 \\
c^{2} & c & 1 \\
d^{2} & d & 1
\end{array}\right|=(b-c)(b-d)(c-d)
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_109b1469a5295e62460dg-1.jpg?height=196&width=718&top_left_y=1165&top_left_x=690)

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =-\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
b^{3}-d^{3} & b-d & 0 \\
c^{3}-d^{3} & c-d & 0 \\
d^{3} & d & 1
\end{array}\right|=-(b-d)(c-d)\left|\begin{array}{cc}
b^{2}+b d+d^{2} & 1 \\
c^{2}+c d+d^{2} & 1
\end{array}\right|= \\
& =-(b-d)(c-d)\left|\begin{array}{cc}
b^{2}-c^{2}+d(b-c) & 0 \\
c^{2}+c d+d^{2} & 1
\end{array}\right|=-(b-c)(b-d)(c-d)(b+c+d)
\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly:

$$
D_{3}=\left|\begin{array}{llll}
a^{3} & a^{2} & 1 & 1 \\
b^{3} & b^{2} & 0 & 1 \\
c^{3} & c^{2} & 0 & 1 \\
d^{3} & d^{2} & 0 & 1
\end{array}\right|=(b-c)(b-d)(c-d)(b c+b d+c d)
$$

and

$$
D_{4}=\left|\begin{array}{llll}
a^{3} & a^{2} & a & 1 \\
b^{3} & b^{2} & b & 0 \\
c^{3} & c^{2} & c & 0 \\
d^{3} & d^{2} & d & 0
\end{array}\right|=-(b-c)(b-d)(c-d) b c d
$$

Thus:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& x=\frac{D_{1}}{D}=\frac{1}{(a-b)(a-c)(a-d)} \\
& y=\frac{D_{2}}{D}=\frac{b+c+d}{(a-b)(a-c)(a-d)} \\
& z=\frac{D_{3}}{D}=\frac{b c+b d+c d}{(a-b)(a-c)(a-d)} \\
& u=\frac{D_{4}}{D}=-\frac{b c d}{(a-b)(a-c)(a-d)}
\end{aligned}
$$

(Imre Kürti, Eger.)

problem: Problem 1. A barrel is filled with water to $\frac{5}{6}$ of its volume. If another 10 liters of water are added to the barrel, it will be filled to $\frac{7}{8}$ of its volume. How many liters of water does the barrel hold?
solution: Solution. Let the barrel collect $x$ liters of water. From the condition of the problem, we have $\frac{5}{6} x+10=\frac{7}{8} x$, that is, $10=\left(\frac{7}{8}-\frac{5}{6}\right) \cdot x$, or $10=\frac{1}{24} \cdot x$, from which $x=24 \cdot 10=240$. Therefore, the barrel collects 240 liters of water.

problem: 16. (15 points) Person A and Person B start climbing a mountain from the bottom along the same path at the same time, and immediately return along the original path after reaching the top. It is known that their descending speeds are three times their respective ascending speeds. A and B meet 150 meters below the summit, and when A returns to the bottom, B is exactly halfway down the mountain. Find the distance from the bottom to the top of the mountain.
solution:
【Solution】Solution one: When they meet 150 meters away from the mountaintop, the distance difference between the two is 200 meters,
the speed ratio of A to B is 8:7,
thus, A's uphill distance is $\frac{200}{2-1} \times 8=1600$,
of these 1600 meters, 50 meters are the result of assuming continued uphill travel,
therefore, the distance from the mountain bottom to the mountaintop $=1600-50=1550$ meters.
Solution two: Let A's uphill speed be $x$, then the downhill speed is $3 x$. B's uphill speed is $y$, then the downhill speed is $3 y$, and the distance from the mountaintop to the mountain bottom is $s$.
$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\frac{s}{x}+\frac{150}{3 x}=\frac{s-150}{y} \text { (1) } \\
\frac{s}{x}+\frac{s}{3 x}=\frac{s}{y}+\frac{0.5 s}{3 y} \text { (2) }
\end{array},\right.
$$

From (1) we get $\frac{s+50}{s-150}=\frac{x}{y}$,
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\text { From (2) we get } \frac{x}{y}=\frac{8}{7}, \\
\therefore \frac{s+50}{s-150}=\frac{8}{7}, \\
\therefore s=1550 \text { (meters), }
\end{array}
$$

In conclusion, the answer is 1550 meters.

problem:
Let's determine the positive integer solutions of the following equation:

$$
x y z + 2 x + 3 y + 6 z = x y + 2 x z + 3 y z
$$
solution:
Let's notice that the first three terms on the left side can be found on the right side either as a $z$-multiple or as a $z$-reciprocal - and these are different terms from each other - so from these term pairs, after reduction to 0, the $(z-1)$ factor can be factored out. If we then subtract 6 from both sides, the entire left side can have the $(z-1)$ factored out:

$$
(z-1)(x y-2 x-3 y+6)=-6
$$

It is easy to further show that the second expression in parentheses can also be factored into a product, so our equation is equivalent to the following:

$$
(x-3)(y-2)(z-1)=-6
$$

Here, all three factors are integers, and since $x, y, z>0$,

$$
x-3 \geq-2, \quad y-2 \geq-1, \quad z-1 \geq 0
$$

The absolute value of the right side can be written as the product of three natural numbers in the following two ways: $6 \cdot 1 \cdot 1$ and $3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1$. Combining these, the possible values for the individual factors are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& (x-3) \text { can be }: \quad-2, \quad-1, \quad 1, \quad 2, \quad 3, \quad 6 \\
& (y-2) \text { can be }: \quad-1, \quad 1,2,3,6 \\
& (z-1) \text { can be }: \quad 1,2,3,6
\end{aligned}
$$

and from these, we need to select one for each factor such that their product is -6.

In the following table, in the subsequent columns, we first list those selections where (1) one of the consecutive factors is 6, and therefore the product of the other two factors is $-1=(-1) \cdot 1=1 \cdot(-1)$, and then those where one factor is 3 and the product of the remaining factors is $-2=(-2) \cdot 1=(-1) \cdot 2$. We immediately wrote down the values of $x, y, z$ as well, and the number of the desired solutions is 10.

$$
$\qquad$

problem:
1. Let $Q(x)=a_{0}+a_{1} x+\cdots+a_{n} x^{n}$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients, and $0 \leq a_{i}<3$ for all $0 \leq i \leq n$.
Given that $Q(\sqrt{3})=20+17 \sqrt{3}$, compute $Q(2)$.
solution:
Answer:
One can evaluate
$$
Q(\sqrt{3})=\left(a_{0}+3 a_{2}+3^{2} a_{4}+\ldots\right)+\left(a_{1}+3 a_{3}+3^{2} a_{5}+\ldots\right) \sqrt{3} .
$$

Therefore, we have that
$$
\left(a_{0}+3 a_{2}+3^{2} a_{4}+\ldots\right)=20 \text { and }\left(a_{1}+3 a_{3}+3^{2} a_{5}+\ldots\right)=17 .
$$

This corresponds to the base- 3 expansions of 20 and 17. This gives us that $Q(x)=2+2 x+2 x^{3}+2 x^{4}+x^{5}$, so $Q(2)=86$.

problem:
## Task 10/88

We are looking for all numbers $n \in N$ that have the following properties:

1. The decimal representation requires exactly three pairwise different digits $a$, $b$, and $c$.
2. Here, $a$ and $b$ each appear exactly $c$ times; $c$, on the other hand, appears $(a-b)$ times.
3. The sum of the digits and the product of the digits of $n$ are equal.
solution:
From the 1st condition, it follows that $a ; b ; c \in N, a ; b ; c \leq 9$, from the 3rd $a ; b ; c>0$. The three conditions can be summarized in the following equation:

$$
a c+b c+c(a-b)=a^{c} b^{c} c^{a-b} \rightarrow 2=a^{c-1} b^{c} c^{a-b-1}
$$

From the uniqueness of the prime factorization, it follows that one of the factors on the right side of the last equation must be equal to 2 and the other two must be equal to 1.

Case distinction:

1. $a^{c-1}=2$ yields $a=2, c=2$ in contradiction to the 1st condition.

Therefore, by the principle of inclusion and exclusion, the sequence after the operation has $M_{100}=100-(33+25)+(8+6+5)-1=60$ (numbers).
This shows that, among the first 100 numbers, after the operation of crossing out numbers as described, 60 numbers remain, i.e., $\frac{3}{5}$ are retained. Therefore, to retain 1988 terms, at least $1988 \div \frac{3}{5} \approx 3314$ terms are needed, i.e., at least the numbers $1,2, \cdots, 3315$ need to be crossed out to possibly obtain $A_{1988}$.

problem: For which integers $h$, are there infinitely many positive integers $n$, such that $\left[n \sqrt{h^{2}+1}\right]$ is a perfect square?
solution:
Obviously, $h=0$ meets the requirement. Next, we prove that any integer $h$ meets the requirement.
Assume $h>0$.
For the equation
$$
\left(h^{2}+1\right) u^{2}-v^{2}=1
$$

with positive integer solutions $(u, v)$, it must be true that
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\left(v^{2}\right)^{2}0$, equation (1) has infinitely many positive integer solutions $(u, v)$.
For any positive integer $m$, we have
$$
\left(\left(\sqrt{h^{2}+1}-h\right)\left(\sqrt{h^{2}+1}+h\right)\right)^{m}=1 \text {. }
$$

For any odd positive integer $l$, the expansion of $\left(\sqrt{h^{2}+1}-h\right)^{l}$ can be written as $\sqrt{h^{2}+1} u_{l}-v_{l}\left(u_{l}, v_{l} \in \mathbf{Z}_{+}\right)$.

Similarly, the expansion of $\left(\sqrt{h^{2}+1}+h\right)^{l}$ can be written as $\sqrt{h^{2}+1} u_{l}+v_{l}$.
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\text { Then }\left(h^{2}+1\right) u_{l}^{2}-v_{l}^{2} \\
=\left(\sqrt{h^{2}+1} u_{l}-v_{l}\right)\left(\sqrt{h^{2}+1} u_{l}+v_{l}\right) \\
=\left(\left(\sqrt{h^{2}+1}-h\right)\left(\sqrt{h^{2}+1}+h\right)\right)^{l}=1 .
\end{array}
$$

This proves that equation (1) has infinitely many positive integer solutions $\left(u_{l}, v_{l}\right)(l=2 k-1)$, thus proving that there are infinitely many positive integers $n_{k}=u_{2 k-1} v_{2 k-1}$, such that
$$
\left[\sqrt{h^{2}+1} n_{k}\right]=v_{2 k-1}^{2} .
$$

problem:
Problem 5.8. There are 7 completely identical cubes, on which 3 points are marked on one face, 2 points on two faces, and 1 point on the rest. These cubes were glued together to form a figure in the shape of the letter "П", as shown in the image, with the number of points on any two adjacent faces being the same.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_6da73bfd3e09e8b55e3fg-13.jpg?height=400&width=519&top_left_y=448&top_left_x=467)

What is on the three left faces $A, B$, and $C$?
solution:
Answer: $A-2, B-2, C-3$.

Solution. For a complete solution to this problem, it is necessary not only to understand how many points are located on the faces of the cube and which of them are adjacent. It is also important to figure out along which exact diagonals the points on the faces of the cube are directed.

Consider the middle right cube (above and below which there are other cubes). On its top face, as well as on its bottom face, there cannot be 3 points (otherwise, the top or bottom cube would have at least two faces with 3 points). Therefore, the face with 3 points is one of the two remaining faces (which are not visible and do not touch anyone). Then, in our cube, opposite the face with 3 points is a face with 2 points, one of the four remaining faces has 2 points, and the other three have 1 point each.

Consider the middle top cube. On its top face, there are 3 points, and on the front face, there are 2 points. It is clear that then on the bottom face of this cube there are 2 points, and on the left face, there is 1 point (Fig. 2).

Consider the middle top cube and the left middle cube. They are identical, so they can be superimposed in space (overlaid on each other). In this case, the faces with three points must coincide; considering the directions of these points, it is clear that this can be done in only two ways; one of these ways is impossible, as otherwise the visible face with 2 points would coincide with the visible face with 1 point. Therefore, the position of the left middle cube is uniquely determined, and on its left face $B$, as well as on the back face, there are 2 points. Then on its top and bottom faces, there is 1 point each.

For the top cube, the top, front, and bottom faces are determined. The right face is also determined - it has 1 point, because the left face of the top middle cube has 1 point. Then on face $A$ there must be 2 points, and on the back face, there are 3 points.

For the bottom cube, there is 1 point on the front and top faces, and 2 points on the right face. Since opposite the face with 3 points cannot be a face with 1 point, we get that on face $C$ there are 3 points.

Thus, on face $A$ there are 2 points, on face $B-2$ points, and on face $C-3$ points. It is not difficult to verify that all 7 cubes can be arranged as shown in the figure so that all the conditions of the problem are satisfied.

224. Boxes with Shells. Shells for six-inch howitzers were packed in boxes of 15, 18, and 20.

- Why do you have different boxes? - I asked the officer at the warehouse.
- You see, - he replied, - this allows us to deliver the required number of shells to the battery without opening the boxes.

Indeed, this system worked flawlessly when a large number of shells was needed, but it proved to be useless if, for example, 5, 10, 25, or 61 shells were required.

What is the largest number of shells that cannot be delivered to the battery in whole boxes, containing 15, 18, and 20 shells each? It is not too large.
solution: 224. An officer at the warehouse must issue the required number of shells in boxes of 18 shells until the remaining number of shells is a multiple of 5. If the number of shells is not 5, 10, or 25, the remaining shells should be issued in boxes of 15 and 20 shells. The largest number of shells for which the system fails is 72 plus 25, that is, 97. If the number of shells in the warehouse is greater, for example, 133, and 108 shells are packed in 6 boxes of 18 shells each, then the officer should issue only 1 box of 18 shells, and the remaining 115 shells should be repackaged into 1 box holding 15 shells and 5 boxes containing 20 shells each. If there are 97 shells in the warehouse, the officer will only have a remainder that is a multiple of 5, that is, 25 shells, after issuing 72 shells.

problem: 4. Let $f(x)=\cos (\cos (\cos (\cos (\cos (\cos (\cos (\cos x)))))))$, and suppose that the number $a$ satisfies the equation $a=\cos a$. Express $f^{\prime}(a)$ as a polynomial in $a$.
solution:
Solution: $\quad a^{8}-4 a^{6}+6 a^{4}-4 a^{2}+1$
This is an exercise using the chain rule. Define $f_{0}(x)=x$ and $f_{n}(x)=\cos f_{n-1}(x)$ for $n \geq 0$. We will show by induction that $f_{n}(a)=a$ and $f_{n}^{\prime}(a)=(-\sin a)^{n}$ for all $n$. The case $n=0$ is clear. Then $f_{n}(a)=\cos f_{n-1}(a)=\cos a=a$, and
$$
f_{n}^{\prime}(a)=f_{n-1}^{\prime}(a) \cdot\left(-\sin f_{n-1}(a)\right)=(-\sin a)^{n-1} \cdot(-\sin a)=(-\sin a)^{n}
$$
by induction. Now, $f(x)=f_{8}(x)$, so $f^{\prime}(a)=(-\sin a)^{8}=\sin ^{8} a$. But $\sin ^{2} a=1-$ $\cos ^{2} a=1-a^{2}$, so $f^{\prime}(a)=\left(1-a^{2}\right)^{4}=a^{8}-4 a^{6}+6 a^{4}-4 a^{2}+1$.

The coefficients of friction between the loads and the shelves are \( \mu_{1}=0.1 \) and \( \mu_{2}=0.2 \). A horizontally directed force \( F=10 \mathrm{H} \) is applied to the center of the pulley. The sliding friction force for the first body:

The sliding friction force for the second body:

## Problem Statement

Calculate the indefinite integral:

$$
\int \frac{4 x^{4}+2 x^{2}-x-3}{x(x-1)(x+1)} d x
$$
solution:
## Solution

$$
\int \frac{4 x^{4}+2 x^{2}-x-3}{x(x-1)(x+1)} d x=\int \frac{4 x^{4}+2 x^{2}-x-3}{x^{3}-x} d x=
$$

The integrand is an improper fraction. Let's separate the integer part:

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
4 x^{4}+2 x^{2}-x-3 & \left\lvert\, \frac{x^{3}-x}{4 x}\right. \\
\frac{4 x^{4}-4 x^{2}}{6 x^{2}-x-3}
\end{array}
$$

We get:

$$
=\int\left(4 x+\frac{6 x^{2}-x-3}{x^{3}-x}\right) d x=\int 4 x d x+\int \frac{6 x^{2}-x-3}{x(x-1)(x+1)} d x=
$$

Let's decompose the proper rational fraction into partial fractions using the method of undetermined coefficients:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{6 x^{2}-x-3}{x(x-1)(x+1)}=\frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{x-1}+\frac{C}{x+1}= \\
& =\frac{A(x-1)(x+1)+B x(x+1)+C x(x-1)}{x(x-1)(x+1)}= \\
& =\frac{A\left(x^{2}-1\right)+B\left(x^{2}+x\right)+C\left(x^{2}-x\right)}{x(x-1)(x+1)}= \\
& =\frac{(A+B+C) x^{2}+(B-C) x-A}{x(x-1)(x+1)}= \\
& \left\{\begin{array}{l}
A+B+C=6 \\
B-C=-1 \\
-A=-3
\end{array}\right.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
B+C=3 \\
B-C=-1 \\
A=3
\end{array}\right.
$$

Add the first row to the second:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left\{\begin{array}{l}
B+C=3 \\
2 B=2 \\
A=3
\end{array}\right. \\
& \left\{\begin{array}{l}
C=2 \\
B=1 \\
A=3
\end{array}\right. \\
& \frac{6 x^{2}-x-3}{x(x-1)(x+1)}=\frac{3}{x}+\frac{1}{x-1}+\frac{2}{x+1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Then we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\int 4 x d x+\int\left(\frac{3}{x}+\frac{1}{x-1}+\frac{2}{x+1}\right) d x= \\
& =2 x^{2}+3 \cdot \ln |x|+\ln |x-1|+2 \cdot \ln |x+1|+C
\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
Exercise 14. We say that two integers $a, b \in \mathbb{N}^{\star}$ are connected if there exists a prime number $p$ such that $\mathrm{a}=\mathrm{pb}$ or $b=\mathrm{pa}$.

Find all integers $n \geqslant 1$ having the following property: one can write all the positive divisors of $n$ (1 and $n$ included) exactly once on a circle in such a way that each divisor is connected to each of its two neighbors?
solution:
Solution to Exercise 14: First, let's consider the case where $n$ has only one prime factor, so $n=p^{\alpha}$. If $\alpha \leqslant 1$, any configuration works. However, if $\alpha \geqslant 2$, 1 must be placed next to two different numbers, and is only connected to one other divisor of $p^{\alpha}$ (which is $p$), so this is not possible.

Notice that the parity of the number of prime factors counted with multiplicity must change between a number and a number that is connected to it. Thus, if $n$ has an odd number of divisors, the existence of such a configuration would imply that 1 has both an even and an odd number of prime factors, which is not possible. The numbers with an odd number of divisors are perfect squares, so they do not satisfy the property stated in the problem.

Now, let's try to solve the case where there are two prime factors, say $n=p^{a} q^{b}$ with one of the numbers $a$ or $b$ being odd, and without loss of generality, assume it is $a$.

The following arrangement works:

$$
1, q, q^{2}, \ldots, q^{b}, p q^{b}, p q^{b-1}, \ldots, p q, p^{2} q, \ldots, p^{a-1} q^{b}, p^{a} q^{b}, p^{a} q^{b-1}, \ldots, p^{a} q, p^{a}, p^{a-1}, \ldots, p, 1
$$

We use the fact that $a$ is odd to say that we have indeed written $p^{a-1} q^{b}$ just before $p^{a} q^{b}$.

We now proceed by induction on the number of prime divisors: suppose we have shown for some $k \geqslant 2$ that all numbers of the form $\prod_{i=1}^{k} p_{i}^{\alpha_{i}}$ with at least one of the $\alpha_{i}$ odd satisfy the property stated in the problem, and let $n=\prod_{i=1}^{k+1} p_{i}^{\alpha_{i}}$ with at least one of the $\alpha_{i}$ odd, say $\alpha_{1}$. Then the induction hypothesis tells us that we can order the divisors of $n'=\prod_{i=1}^{k} p_{i}^{\alpha_{i}}$ as $d_{1}, \ldots d_{m}$ such that $d_{i}$ and $d_{i+1}$ are all connected, as well as $d_{m}$ and $d_{1}$. Then the following arrangement works for $m$ (since $m$ is even):

$$
d_{1}, p_{k+1} d_{1}, \ldots, p_{k+1}^{\alpha_{k+1}} d_{1}, p_{k+1}^{\alpha_{k+1}} d_{2}, \ldots p_{k+1} d_{2}, d_{2}, d_{3}, \ldots, p_{k+1}^{\alpha_{k+1}} d_{m}, \ldots p_{k+1} d_{m}, d_{m}, d_{1}
$$

Thus, the numbers that do not satisfy this property are the squares (different from 1) and the powers (greater than 2) of prime numbers.

Comment from the graders: The exercise, which is somewhat combinatorial, is relatively less treated but generally well succeeded by the students who approached it. Most students who have the intuition of the construction to be carried out for composite numbers have difficulty formulating it rigorously (by induction).

problem:

solution:
None of the rooks standing in the corner squares can be taken. Indeed, at the moment when the first of them is taken, it is attacked by exactly two rooks. Suppose it was possible to leave only the four corner rooks. Then the last rook taken was either attacked by two rooks (if it stood on the edge of the board), or by none. Contradiction. Therefore, at least five rooks will remain.

We will show how to take 59 rooks. First, we will take all the rooks from the 8th rank, except for three - a8, b8, and h8, then repeat the same with the 7th, 6th, ..., 3rd, and 1st ranks (skipping the 2nd). Now we will take the rooks from the 1st file from a3 to a7, and from the last file from h3 to h7. Next, we will take the rooks b1 and a2. Finally, we will sequentially take the rooks from b8 to b3 and from g2 to c2.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_d3d405875929faed9b27g-09.jpg?height=52&width=300&top_left_y=400&top_left_x=-1)  Among 49 students, each is acquainted with at least 25 others.  Prove that they can be divided into groups of two or three such that each is acquainted with everyone in their group.}

## Solution

Imagine that initially all 49 students are standing in a corridor, and we will gradually let them into the classroom. We will do this in such a way that at any moment in the classroom, the children are divided into the required groups. Let Fyodor be a student standing in the corridor. If he is acquainted with another student standing in the corridor, we will simply let them both into the classroom. Otherwise, all of Fyodor's acquaintances are already in the classroom. Since there are fewer than 50 students in the classroom, they are divided into fewer than 25 groups. Therefore, among Fyodor's acquaintances, some two are in the same group. If this is a group of two students, we will let Fyodor into the classroom, adding him to this group. If it is a group of three students, we will ask one of Fyodor's acquaintances to form a group with him, and leave the remaining students in a pair.

By gradually letting students into the classroom, we will achieve that all students are divided into the required groups.

problem: Problem 2. Three professors wrote a collection of math problems and divided the honorarium in the ratio 8:6:5. If the honorarium had been divided in the ratio 7:5:4, one of the professors would have received 250 denars more than he received in the first division. How much did each of the authors receive?
solution:
Solution. Let the total honorarium received by the three professors be $x$ denars. Then the first professor received $\frac{8}{19} x$ denars, the second $\frac{6}{19} x$ denars, and the third $\frac{5}{19} x$ denars. Since $\frac{8}{19} < \frac{7}{16}$ and $\frac{5}{19} > \frac{4}{16}$, it follows that with the second distribution, the first professor would receive 250 denars more than with the first distribution, i.e.,
$\frac{7}{16} x - \frac{8}{19} x = 250$). From this, $x = 15200$. Therefore, the first professor received 6400 denars, the second 4800 denars, and the third 4000 denars.

x^{2}+y^{2}=b

given that $x>0$, there is a unique solution.
solution: Solution. Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2}=\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$ be the set of pairs $(x, y)$ that satisfy system (1) with $x>0$. From $x^{2}+y^{2}=b$ it follows that $b>0$. If $(x, y) \in S$, then $(x,-y) \in S$, which means that for system (1) to have a unique solution, given $x>0$, it must be $y=0$ and $a=0$. problem: Problem 1. If $x+y=0$ and $x^{2}+y^{2}=\frac{1}{4}$, calculate the sum $x^{4}+y^{4}$.
solution:
Solution. If $x+y=0$, then $(x+y)^{2}=0$, i.e., $2 x y=-(x^{2}+y^{2})$, so $2 x y=-\frac{1}{4}$, which means $x y=-\frac{1}{8}$. According to this,

$$
x^{4}+y^{4}=\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{2}-2 x^{2} y^{2}=\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{2}-2\left(-\frac{1}{8}\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{16}-\frac{2}{64}=\frac{1}{32}
$$

problem: On a matchbox, we want to paint two sides red, two sides yellow, and two sides blue. How many ways can this be done? How many ways can a cube be painted like this?
solution:
The matching color pairs on the box can either be adjacent, meaning they share an edge, or parallel. For the purpose of classifying coloring possibilities, the first criterion we consider is how many of the three pairs of parallel faces of the box are painted in matching colors. It is clear that it can be painted in such a way that there are no such pairs, or only one, and if we have already painted two pairs in this manner, then the third one will also be, so this number $p=3$, or 1, or 0.

1. Let $p=3$. This uniquely determines the painting of the cube. Thus, in all 8 vertices, 3 different colors meet, and the only difference between two vertices is that if we turn the vertex towards ourselves, the 3 colors, when moving clockwise, are either $p$ (red), $s$ (yellow), $k$ (blue) or $p, k, s$. If we now choose this order at one vertex during painting, this already determines the entire painting of the cube, and in the 3 vertices adjacent to the selected vertex, the reverse order will appear (Figure 1, 4 light and 4 dark circles indicate the matching orientations).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_187718e1cf592f2dae1cg-1.jpg?height=505&width=555&top_left_y=585&top_left_x=774)

Figure 1

We also considered that the two sets of four vertices can be transformed into each other, for example, by a $90^{\circ}$ rotation around the axis connecting the centers of the horizontal faces (in either direction).

The matchbox has three different faces: a large rectangle with the label, a long rectangle with the hinge, and a small rectangle, which is the visible inner part of the box (briefly $N, H$, and $K$ faces). The two parallel $N$-shaped faces can be colored in 3 different ways, then the $H$-shaped faces can be colored in 2 different ways from the two remaining colors, and this uniquely determines the color of the $K$-shaped faces. Thus, we get $3 \cdot 2=6$ different colorings, and these are all different, since among them, for any two, there is an $N, H, K$ face whose color is different in one coloring compared to the other.

2. Now let $p=1$ and paint the base and top faces of the cube in the same color - $a$ color. Then, by rotating around the vertical face axis, the order of the other two colors can only be $b, b, c, c, b, b, c, \ldots$, and we can choose any face as the front face, so the "letter plan" of the painting is unique. From this, we get 3 differently painted cubes, depending on which color we choose.

For the matchbox, the pair of faces painted in the same color can be chosen in 3 ways. If we have already chosen this (let's say the $N$-shaped faces are the same color) and also chosen the color of this face (for which we have 3 options now), the two remaining colors must be used for the $H$-shaped and $K$-shaped faces, and we can only decide on the order in which we connect the colorings of these two faces (by rotating the box around the axis perpendicular to the $N$-shaped faces). However, the two possible colorings do not differ from each other, because if we hold the box so that the $N$-shaped faces are horizontal, and then flip the bottom face to the top, the two colorings transform into each other. Therefore, the matchbox has $3 \cdot 3=9$ possible colorings when $p=1$.

3. Finally, in the case of $p=0$, each of the three colors appears twice, meeting at an edge, let this be the red color on the front edge $B J$ of the top face of the cube (Figure 2).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_187718e1cf592f2dae1cg-1.jpg?height=566&width=436&top_left_y=2075&top_left_x=823)

Figure 2

Then the third face that meets at $B$ and $J$, i.e., the left and right side faces, must be different. It does not matter whether we paint the right face yellow or blue, and the left face blue or yellow, because these two faces can be transformed into each other by a $180^{\circ}$ rotation around the axis passing through the midpoint of the $B J$ edge, the cube returns to its initial position, and the two red faces are swapped. So let the right side face be yellow and the left side face be blue. Of the remaining 2 faces, the second yellow one can be the bottom or the back, and these 2 options are different and uniquely determine the position of the second blue face.

According to this, the cube can be painted in $1+3+2=6$ different ways while meeting the requirements of the problem.

For the matchbox, the red pair and edge can be chosen in 3 ways: $N$ and $H$ face, $N$ and $K$, $H$ and $K$ face common edge. Furthermore, we cannot transform the two red faces into each other by the mentioned $180^{\circ}$ rotation, so the number of possibilities is multiplied by 3 and 2, resulting in $2 \cdot 3 \cdot 2=12$.

Therefore, the box can be painted in $6+9+12=27$ different ways.

László Pálffy (Pécs, Széchenyi I. Gymnasium, 2nd grade)

problem:
## Problem Statement

Find the indefinite integral:

$$
\int \frac{3 x^{3}+x+46}{(x-1)^{2}\left(x^{2}+9\right)} d x
$$
solution:
## Solution

$$
\int \frac{3 x^{3}+x+46}{(x-1)^{2}\left(x^{2}+9\right)} d x=
$$

We decompose the proper rational fraction into partial fractions using the method of undetermined coefficients:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{3 x^{3}+x+46}{(x-1)^{2}\left(x^{2}+9\right)}=\frac{A_{1}}{x-1}+\frac{A_{2}}{(x-1)^{2}}+\frac{B x+C}{x^{2}+9}= \\
& =\frac{A_{1}(x-1)\left(x^{2}+9\right)+A_{2}\left(x^{2}+9\right)+(B x+C)(x-1)^{2}}{(x-1)^{2}\left(x^{2}+9\right)}= \\
& =\frac{A_{1}\left(x^{3}-x^{2}+9 x-9\right)+A_{2}\left(x^{2}+9\right)+B\left(x^{3}-2 x^{2}+x\right)+C\left(x^{2}-2 x+1\right)}{(x-1)^{2}\left(x^{2}+9\right)}= \\
& =\frac{\left(A_{1}+B\right) x^{3}+\left(-A_{1}+A_{2}-2 B+C\right) x^{2}+\left(9 A_{1}+B-2 C\right) x+\left(-9 A_{1}+9 A_{2}+C\right)}{(x-1)^{2}\left(x^{2}+9\right)} \\
& \left\{\begin{array}{l}
A_{1}+B=3 \\
-A_{1}+A_{2}-2 B+C=0 \\
9 A_{1}+B-2 C=1 \\
-9 A_{1}+9 A_{2}+C=46
\end{array}\right.
\end{aligned}
$$

Add the second equation multiplied by -9 to the fourth equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left\{\begin{array}{l}
A_{1}+B=3 \\
-A_{1}+A_{2}-2 B+C=0 \\
9 A_{1}+B-2 C=1 \\
18 B-8 C=46
\end{array}\right. \\
& \left\{\begin{array}{l}
A_{1}+B=3 \\
-A_{1}+A_{2}-2 B+C=0 \\
9 A_{1}+B-2 C=1 \\
9 B-4 C=23
\end{array}\right.
\end{aligned}
$$

Add the third equation multiplied by -2 to the fourth equation:

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
A_{1}+B=3 \\
-A_{1}+A_{2}-2 B+C=0 \\
9 A_{1}+B-2 C=1 \\
-18 A_{1}+7 B=21
\end{array}\right.
$$

Add the first equation multiplied by 18 to the fourth equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left\{\begin{array}{l}
A_{1}+B=3 \\
-A_{1}+A_{2}-2 B+C=0 \\
9 A_{1}+B-2 C=1 \\
25 B=75
\end{array}\right. \\
& \left\{\begin{array}{l}
A_{1}=0 \\
-A_{1}+A_{2}+C=6 \\
9 A_{1}-2 C=-2 \\
B=3
\end{array}\right. \\
& \left\{\begin{array}{l}
A_{1}=0 \\
A_{2}+C=6 \\
-2 C=-2 \\
B=3
\end{array}\right. \\
& \left\{\begin{array}{l}
A_{1}=0 \\
A_{2}=5 \\
C=1 \\
B=3
\end{array}\right. \\
& \frac{3 x^{3}+x+46}{(x-1)^{2}\left(x^{2}+9\right)}=\frac{5}{(x-1)^{2}}+\frac{3 x+1}{x^{2}+9}
\end{aligned}
$$

Then:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \int \frac{3 x^{3}+x+46}{(x-1)^{2}\left(x^{2}+9\right)} d x=\int\left(\frac{5}{(x-1)^{2}}+\frac{3 x+1}{x^{2}+9}\right) d x= \\
& =\int \frac{5}{(x-1)^{2}} d x+\int \frac{3 x+1}{x^{2}+9} d x=-\frac{5}{x-1}+\int \frac{3 x}{x^{2}+9} d x+\int \frac{1}{x^{2}+9} d x= \\
& =-\frac{5}{x-1}+\frac{3}{2} \cdot \int \frac{d\left(x^{2}+9\right)}{x^{2}+9}+\frac{1}{3} \cdot \operatorname{arctg}\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)=-\frac{5}{x-1}+\frac{3}{2} \cdot \ln \left(x^{2}+9\right)+\frac{1}{3} \cdot \operatorname{arctg}\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)+C
\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
Bogdanov I.i.

Find all such pairs of distinct real numbers $x$ and $y$ that $x^{100}-y^{100}=2^{99}(x-y)$ and $x^{200}-y^{200}=$ $2^{199}(x-y)$
solution:
For convenience, let's make the substitution $x=2a$ and $y=2b$. Then $a^{100}-b^{100}=a^{200}-b^{200}=a-b \neq 0$. Dividing the second expression by the first, we get

$a^{100}+b^{100}=1$; hence, each of the numbers $a$ and $b$ in absolute value does not exceed 1.

If $b=0$, then $a^{100}=a$, from which $a=1$. Similarly, if $a=0$, then $b=1$.

Now let $ab \neq 0$; then $0a^{100}+b^{100}=1$. Contradiction.

## Answer

$(2,0)$ and $(0,2)$.

$$

$$

3rd Putnam 1940 Problem B5 Find all rational triples (a, b, c) for which a, b, c are the roots of x 3 + ax 2 + bx + c = 0. Solution Straightforward.
solution: : (0, 0, 0); (1, -1, -1), (1, -2, 0). We require (1) a + b + c = -a, (2) ab + bc + ca = b, and (3) abc = -c. From (3), either c = 0, or ab = -1. If c = 0, then (1) becomes b = -2a, and (2) becomes b(a - 1) = 0. Hence either a = b = 0, or a = 1, b = -2. So assume c ≠ 0, and ab = -1. (1) becomes c = - b - 2a. Substituting in (2), we get: -1 - (2a + b)(a + b) = b, so -a 2 -2a 4 + 3a 2 - 1 = -a, or 2a 4 - 2a 2 - a + 1 = 0. So a = 1, or 2a 3 + 2a 2 - 1 = 0 (*). The first possibility gives a = 1, b = -1, c = -1. Suppose a = m/n is a root of (*) with m, n relatively prime integers. Then 2m 3 + 2m 2 n - n 3 = 0. So any prime factor of n must divide 2 and any prime factor of m must divide 1. Hence the only possibilities are a = 1, -1, 1/2, -1/2, and we easily check that these are not solutions. problem:
1097. Solve the equations:
1) $y^{\prime \prime \prime}=60 x^{2}$. 2) $(x-3) y^{\prime \prime}+y^{\prime}=0$
2) $y y^{\prime \prime}-\left(y^{\prime}\right)^{2}=y^{3}$, if $y(0)=-\frac{1}{2}, y^{\prime}(0)=0$.
solution:
Solution. 1) Multiplying both sides of the given third-order equation by $d x$ and then integrating, we obtain a second-order equation: $y^{\prime \prime \prime} d x=60 x^{2} d x ; y^{\prime \prime}=20 x^{3}+C_{1}$.

Next, using the same method, we obtain a first-order equation and then the sought function - the general integral of the given equation:

$$
\begin{gathered}
y^{\prime \prime} d x=20 x^{3} d x+C_{1} d x ; \quad y^{\prime}=5 x^{4}+C_{1} x+C_{2} \\
y^{\prime} d x=\left(5 x^{4}+C_{1} x+C_{2}\right) d x ; \quad y=x^{5}+C_{1} \frac{x^{2}}{2}+C_{2} x+C_{3}
\end{gathered}
$$

2) The given second-order equation does not contain the function $y$ explicitly. Let $y^{\prime}=p$, then $y^{\prime \prime}=\frac{d p}{d x}$ and after substitution, the given equation turns into a first-order equation:

$$
(x-3) \frac{d p}{d x}+p=0
$$

Separating variables and integrating, we find $\frac{d \rho}{p}+\frac{d x}{x-3}=0$; $\ln |p|+\ln |x-3|=\ln C ; \quad|p(x-3)|=C ; \quad p(x-3)= \pm C=C_{\mathbf{1}}$.

Replacing the auxiliary variable $p$ with $\frac{d y}{d x}$, we obtain the equation $(x-3) \frac{d y}{d x}=C_{1}$, solving which we find the sought general integral:

$$
d y=\frac{C_{1} d x}{x-3} ; y=C_{1} \ln |x-3|+C_{2}
$$

3) This is an incomplete second-order equation, not containing the argument $x$ explicitly. Let $y^{\prime}=p$; then $y^{\prime \prime}=p \frac{d p}{d y}$ and the given equation transforms into a first-order equation:

$$
y p \frac{d p}{d y}-p^{2}=y^{3} \quad \text { or } \quad \frac{d p}{d y}-\frac{p}{y}=\frac{y^{2}}{\rho},
$$

which is a Bernoulli equation if $p$ is considered as a function of $y$.

Substituting the function using the formula $\rho=u v$, we have

$$
u \frac{d v}{d y}+v \frac{d u}{d y}-\frac{u v}{y}=\frac{u^{2}}{u v} \quad \text { or } \quad u \frac{d v}{d y}+v\left(\frac{d u}{d y}-\frac{u}{y}\right)=\frac{y^{2}}{u v}
$$

From this, to find $u$ and $v$, we obtain two equations:

$$
\frac{d u}{d y}-\frac{u}{y}=0 \quad \text { and } \quad u \frac{d v}{d y}=\frac{y^{2}}{u v}
$$

From the first equation, we find $u$, as its simplest particular integral:

$$
\frac{d u}{u}-\frac{d y}{y}=0 ; \quad \ln u=\ln y ; \quad u=y
$$

Substituting $u$ into the second equation, we find $v$, as its general integral:

$$
y \frac{d v}{d y}=\frac{y^{2}}{y v} ; \quad v d v=d y ; \quad \frac{v^{2}}{2}=y+C_{1} ; \quad v= \pm \sqrt{2\left(y+C_{1}\right)}
$$

Knowing $u$ and $v$, we find $p=u v= \pm y \sqrt{2\left(y+C_{1}\right)}$.

Replacing $p$ with $\frac{d y}{d x}$, we obtain a separable variable equation

$$
\frac{d y}{d x}= \pm y \sqrt{2\left(y+C_{1}\right)}
$$

Before integrating this equation, it is advisable to determine the value of the constant $C_{1}$ using the given values $y=-\frac{1}{2}, \quad y^{\prime}=0$ :

$$
0= \pm \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{2\left(-\frac{1}{2}+C_{1}\right)} ; \quad C_{1}=\frac{1}{2}
$$

Substituting the value of $C_{1}$ into the last equation, separating the variables, and integrating, we find

$$
\frac{d y}{y \sqrt{2 y+1}}= \pm d x ; \quad \pm x+C_{2}=\int \frac{d y}{y \sqrt{2 y+1}}=I
$$

To find the integral $I$, let $\sqrt{2!+1}=2$, then $2 y+1=z^{2}, d y=z d z$

$$
I=2 \int \frac{d z}{z^{2}-1}=\ln \left|\frac{z-1}{z+1}\right|=\ln \frac{|\sqrt{2 y+1}-1|}{\sqrt{2 y+1}+1}
$$

Therefore,

$$
C_{2} \pm x=\ln \frac{|1-\sqrt{2 y+1}|}{1+\sqrt{2 y+1}}
$$

Finally, using the given values $x=0, y=\frac{1}{2}$, we determine the value of the constant $C_{2}==\ln |-1|=0$ and obtain the sought
particular integral

$$
x= \pm \ln \frac{|1-\sqrt{2 y+1}|}{1+\sqrt{2 y+1}}
$$

As shown in the solution of this problem, when finding particular integrals of higher-order equations (of the specified types), there is no need to first find the general integral and then determine the values of all constants. It is better to determine the value of each constant immediately after it appears in the solution process.

problem: 12. The teacher is buying souvenirs for the students. There are three different types of souvenirs in the store (souvenirs of the same type are identical), priced at 1 yuan, 2 yuan, and 4 yuan respectively. The teacher plans to spend 101 yuan, and at least one of each type of souvenir must be purchased. There are $\qquad$ different purchasing schemes.
solution: Let the number of souvenirs purchased at prices of 1 yuan, 2 yuan, and 4 yuan be $x, y, z$ respectively, then $x+2 y+4 z=101$. When $z=1$, $x+2 y=97, y=1,2, \cdots, 48 ;$ when $z=2$, $x+2 y=93, y=1,2, \cdots, 46$; when $z=3$, $x+2 y=89, y=1,2, \cdots, 44 ; \cdots,$ when $z=24$, $x+2 y=5, y=1,2$. Therefore, there are $2+4+\cdots+48=\frac{24 \times 50}{2}=600$ different purchasing schemes.

solution:
Such a path can be drawn exactly when there are either exactly zero or exactly two points in the network where an odd number of lines meet.

(At such a point, one can only start or end, since for each line one reaches a point, one also needs another line to leave it again. The number of lines that meet at a point that is neither the start nor the endpoint of the path must therefore be even. On the other hand, a connected structure where, except for possibly two points, an even number of lines meet at all points, can always be drawn as a continuous path.)

In network (1), there are 6 points where 3 lines meet, in network (2) there are 4, in network (3) also 4, in network (4) there are 6, in networks (5) and (6) there are exactly 2 each, in network (7) there are 6, in network (8) there are 4, in network (9) exactly 2, in network (10) there are 4, and in network (11) again exactly 2. Therefore, only the networks (5), (6), (9), and (11) can be drawn in a single path.

In each of these networks, the two points where three lines meet are the starting and ending points of the corresponding path.

Remark: In the context of graph theory, the lines are considered as edges and their endpoints as nodes. The question of whether all edges can be combined into a path that contains each edge exactly once is also referred to as the question of whether the graph contains an Eulerian path. (See the Seven Bridges of Königsberg problem.)

problem: 3. Find the non-zero natural numbers $n \in \mathbb{N}^{*}$, for which the sum $S=2^{n}+4^{n}+6^{n}+\ldots+1888^{n}$ is divisible by 10.
solution:
Solution.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& U\left(2^{n}\right)= \begin{cases}6, & n=4 k \quad k \in \mathbb{N}^{*} \\
2, & n=4 k+1 \\
4, & n=4 k+2 \\
8, & n=4 k+3\end{cases} \\
